title: Fabric Delivery Phase Gates: Environments, CI/CD, Testing, Security, Operational Readiness
purpose: Sequences a Fabric implementation into five evidence-gated delivery phases so a workload cannot reach production on confidence alone — environments, CI/CD, testing, security, and operational readiness must each show proof before the next gate opens.
accessibleSummary: A five-gate decision path read left to right. Gate 1 checks that isolated, Git-integrated Dev/Test/Prod workspaces exist. Gate 2 checks that Deployment Pipelines promote items with Variable Library environment binding and a pull-request gate. Gate 3 checks that pipeline reliability — retries and idempotent Delta MERGE writes — is actually tested, not assumed. Gate 4 checks that secrets are vaulted and identities scoped to least privilege. Gate 5 checks that Item Recovery and a support owner are proven before general availability. Any gate that fails routes back into that same phase for remediation rather than letting the workload advance with a gap, and a feedback edge shows configuration drift discovered in production re-opening the environments gate.
longDescription: This decision path operationalizes 'implementing a Fabric architecture' as a sequence of five gates rather than a single go-live decision. Each gate pairs a sourced Fabric capability with a recommended delivery practice: workspace types and capacity SKUs gate which experiences can run (a product fact), while Deployment Pipelines with Variable Libraries, pull-request approval, retry-with-backoff, idempotent MERGE writes, vaulted secrets, and service-principal authentication are recommended patterns drawn from Fabric CI/CD tooling and published pipeline-hardening guidance rather than product guarantees. The final gate treats Fabric's built-in Item Recovery restore path as the operational-readiness proof point: if a team cannot demonstrate a tested restore and a named support owner, the pattern is not ready to scale even if every earlier gate passed. The five phases are deliberately sequential and gated, not parallel checklists, because a CI/CD pipeline built before environments are isolated, or security hardening applied after go-live, both routinely fail to catch the class of defect the phase was meant to prevent.

nodes.label: Gate 1 — Environments ready?
nodes.summary: Confirms isolated Dev, Test, and Production workspaces exist, each backed by the workspace type its experiences require, with Git integration enabled.
nodes.detail: Environment readiness means separate workspaces for Dev, Test, and Production rather than folders or naming conventions inside one workspace. Each workspace's type (its former license mode) determines which capacity backs it — Fabric F SKU, Power BI Premium P SKU, or a shared Pro/PPU pool — and only Fabric, Trial, and P-SKU workspace types support the full set of Fabric experiences, so a Pro-only workspace silently blocks some item types. Fabric enables Git integration by default for newly created items, storing item definitions as plain-text files that are diffable and revertible, which is the mechanism the later CI/CD gate depends on.
nodes.whyItMatters: Treating environments as a naming convention inside one workspace, rather than isolated workspaces with their own capacity and Git history, is the single most common reason a later promotion or rollback has no safe place to happen.

evidence.note: A workspace's type dictates which kind of capacity backs it — Fabric F SKU, Power BI Premium P SKU, or the shared Pro/PPU pools — and therefore which experiences its users can run; only Fabric, Trial, and P-SKU workspace types support all Fabric experiences.

Git integration is enabled by default for newly created Fabric items (Dataflow Gen2, pipelines, notebooks, semantic models, Eventstreams), with item definitions stored as plain-text files that are diffable and revertible.

inputs: Named Dev, Test, and Production workspace plan
processing: Provision isolated workspaces per environment
Confirm workspace type supports the experiences the workload needs
Connect each workspace to Git and verify item definitions serialize as plain text
outputs: Three isolated, Git-backed workspaces
A documented capacity/SKU mapping
A verified diff-and-revert path for item changes
drill.example: A finance workload's Dev workspace runs on a trial capacity for iteration; Test and Production are promoted to F-SKU workspaces sized for their real load, and every item — pipeline, notebook, semantic model — is tracked in the same Git repository with per-environment branches.
failureModes: Dev and Prod sharing one workspace with folder-based separation
A Pro-only workspace silently rejecting an item type mid-project
Items created without Git tracking, breaking later diff and rollback

nodes.label: Gate 2 — CI/CD wired?
nodes.summary: Confirms Deployment Pipelines promote items across Dev, Test, and Production with Variable Library environment binding and a pull-request gate before Production.
nodes.detail: Fabric Data Factory is framed as a cloud-native, serverless orchestration environment with built-in CI/CD and deployment capabilities, and fabric-cicd — Microsoft's own Fabric CI/CD deployment tooling — is the same item-deployment engine used both by programmatic pipelines and by Microsoft's own Jumpstart installer, rather than a bespoke or third-party mechanism. Published implementation guidance recommends using Deployment Pipelines to promote items across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces, using Variable Libraries to inject environment-specific connection strings instead of hardcoding them per environment, and requiring a pull-request gate before anything promotes to Production.
nodes.whyItMatters: Promotion without a Variable Library forces environment-specific values to be hand-edited at each stage, and promotion without a pull-request gate means a change reaches Production the moment someone clicks promote, with no independent review step.

evidence.note: Fabric Data Factory is framed as a cloud-native, serverless orchestration environment that auto-scales its underlying compute and includes built-in CI/CD and deployment capabilities for multi-cloud pipeline solutions.

Recommended deployment pattern: Deployment Pipelines promote items across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces, with Variable Libraries injecting environment-specific connection strings, and pull-request gates required before promotion to production.

inputs: A defined Dev → Test → Production pipeline stage order
processing: Assign each workspace to a Deployment Pipeline stage
Bind Variable Libraries per stage so connection strings and parameters switch automatically
Require pull-request approval before the Production promotion step executes
outputs: A repeatable, auditable promotion path
Environment-correct configuration with no manual edits
A review checkpoint immediately before Production
drill.example: A pipeline promoted from Test to Production automatically picks up the Production Variable Library's warehouse connection string; the promotion itself is blocked until a second engineer approves the pull request.
failureModes: Hardcoded connection strings copy-pasted between environments
Promotion to Production with no required reviewer
fabric-cicd or Deployment Pipelines used for only some item types, leaving others manually copied

nodes.label: Gate 3 — Reliability tested?
nodes.summary: Confirms pipeline failure handling — retries with exponential backoff and idempotent Delta MERGE writes — is actually exercised, not just designed.
nodes.detail: Published guidance recommends a pipeline reliability pattern of three retries with exponential backoff for transient failures, combined with idempotent write logic using Delta MERGE instead of a plain INSERT, so that a rerun after a failure does not create duplicate records. This gate is about proving the pattern under a real forced failure — killing a run mid-pipeline and rerunning it — rather than trusting that the configuration exists.
nodes.whyItMatters: A retry policy that has never actually fired, or a MERGE key that silently allows duplicates on a partial key match, both look correct in code review and both fail exactly when a transient outage makes them matter most.

evidence.note: Recommended pipeline reliability pattern: three retries with exponential backoff for transient failures, combined with idempotent write logic (Delta MERGE instead of plain INSERT) so reruns do not create duplicate records.

inputs: A defined retry and backoff configuration
A MERGE key that uniquely identifies each record
processing: Force a transient failure mid-run in Test
Confirm the configured retries fire with increasing backoff
Rerun the full pipeline and verify row counts show no duplication
outputs: Evidence the retry policy actually executes
Evidence a full rerun is safe
A documented, exercised failure-recovery procedure
drill.example: An engineer kills a notebook activity after it has written half its output, then reruns the pipeline; the MERGE key ensures the already-written rows are updated in place rather than duplicated, and the run completes without manual cleanup.
failureModes: INSERT-only writes that duplicate rows on any rerun
A MERGE key that is not actually unique, silently overwriting unrelated rows
Retries configured but never tested against a real transient failure

nodes.label: Gate 4 — Security hardened?
nodes.summary: Confirms connection secrets live only in linked-service-backed key vaults, Notebook activities authenticate as a service principal or workspace identity, and permissions are scoped to specific items rather than workspace Admin.
nodes.detail: Recommended pipeline security hardening keeps connection secrets exclusively in linked-service-backed key vaults rather than inline in a pipeline or notebook, authenticates Notebook activities through a service principal or workspace identity instead of a user's own credentials, and scopes that identity's permissions to the specific OneLake items it needs rather than granting workspace Admin. This gate also has to account for AI surfaces: because agents and Copilot operate within the querying user's own permissions rather than a separate service identity, the access controls set here directly and automatically constrain what an AI experience can retrieve, without any AI-specific configuration.
nodes.whyItMatters: A service principal granted workspace Admin to save configuration time becomes the same over-broad identity every downstream Copilot or agent query inherits, since AI surfaces run under the querying user's own permissions rather than a narrower service identity.

evidence.note: Recommended pipeline security hardening: connection secrets only in linked-service-backed key vaults (never inline), Notebook activities authenticated via service principal or workspace identity rather than user credentials, service principal permissions scoped to specific OneLake items instead of workspace Admin.

Because agents and Copilot operate within the querying user's own permissions rather than a separate service identity, tightening access controls on the underlying data directly constrains what an AI experience can retrieve and surface, without any AI-specific configuration.

inputs: An inventory of connection secrets and identities in use
A target least-privilege role assignment per identity
processing: Move every inline secret into a linked-service-backed key vault
Switch Notebook activity authentication from user credentials to a service principal or workspace identity
Scope that identity's role to the specific items it touches, removing workspace Admin
outputs: No inline secrets remaining in any item definition
Service-identity authentication on every automated activity
An access boundary that also bounds what Copilot and agents can surface
drill.example: A notebook that previously ran under a data engineer's personal credentials, with a database password pasted into a cell, is switched to a workspace identity reading its connection from a vaulted linked service scoped only to the lakehouse it needs.
failureModes: Inline secrets surviving in an old notebook cell or pipeline parameter
A service principal granted workspace Admin instead of an item-scoped role
Copilot surfacing sensitive rows because the underlying data access was never scoped down

nodes.label: Gate 5 — Operations proven?
nodes.summary: Confirms Item Recovery restore is tested and a support owner is confirmed before the pattern is treated as generally available.
nodes.detail: Fabric's Item Recovery lets deleted items be restored either through the Workspace Recycle Bin in the portal UI or programmatically via a REST API, with tenant admins able to configure a retention window of up to 90 days and adjust it at any time. GA guidance recommends tenant admins review and confirm the Item Recovery tenant setting against organizational policy as an explicit operational rollout step, and organizations using automation for audit or compliance are advised to integrate Item Recovery's REST APIs and audit events into existing governance workflows rather than treating restore as a manual, ad hoc action.
nodes.whyItMatters: A retention window and a restore API existing in the product is not the same as a team having exercised the restore path and knowing who owns it; the gap is invisible until the first accidental deletion in Production.

evidence.note: Deleted items can be restored either through the Workspace Recycle bin in the portal UI or programmatically via a REST API.
Tenant admins can configure a retention window of up to 90 days for Item Recovery and can adjust that window at any time.

inputs: A security-hardened, tested pipeline from Gate 4
The tenant's configured Item Recovery retention window
A named support owner and escalation route
processing: Delete a non-critical test item and confirm restore via both the Recycle Bin UI and the REST API
Confirm the retention window matches organizational policy
Confirm the named support owner can execute the restore procedure without escalation
outputs: A demonstrated, working restore path
A retention window matched to policy, not left at the default
General-availability sign-off for the pattern
drill.example: Before go-live, the support owner deliberately deletes a duplicate test semantic model, restores it from the Recycle Bin within minutes, then repeats the restore using the REST API to prove the automation path works too.
controls: Recycle Bin and REST API restore procedure
Named support owner and escalation route
failureModes: Retention window left at a default that does not match compliance requirements
Restore procedure documented but never actually executed
No single owner accountable when the first real deletion happens

nodes.label: Remediation loop
nodes.summary: Any gate that fails routes back into that same phase for hardening rather than letting the workload advance with an unresolved gap.
nodes.detail: The remediation loop is the architectural stance that a failed gate is a stop condition for that phase, not a note to revisit later. A workload does not skip ahead to CI/CD because environments are 'mostly' ready, and it does not reach operational readiness because security was 'probably' fine — each phase must independently pass before the next opens.
nodes.whyItMatters: Allowing a phase to pass on partial evidence is how a known gap in one phase becomes an unexplained production incident two phases later, once the missing context has been lost.

inputs: The specific unmet criterion from that phase
processing: Stop promotion of the workload past the failed gate
Assign the remediation to an owner within that phase
Re-run the same gate check after remediation
outputs: A closed gap with evidence, not a waived checklist item
A workload that only advances once every prior gate independently passes
drill.example: A workload fails Gate 4 because a notebook still authenticates with a personal account; the team fixes the identity and re-runs Gate 4 rather than proceeding to Gate 5 with a tracked exception.
failureModes: Gaps tracked as backlog items while the workload proceeds anyway
A gate re-checked by the same person who waived it the first time, with no independent verification

nodes.label: Production drift feedback
nodes.summary: Configuration drift discovered in Production re-opens Gate 1 (environments) rather than being patched in place.
nodes.detail: Because Gate 1 establishes the isolated, Git-tracked environment baseline every later gate depends on, drift discovered in Production — a manually edited item, an untracked permission change, a capacity reassignment made outside the promotion path — has to be resolved by reconciling the environment against its Git-tracked definition, not by a one-off manual fix that leaves the drift undocumented.
nodes.whyItMatters: A manual patch applied directly in Production without going back through the environments gate reintroduces exactly the untracked, non-reproducible state the whole gated path was built to prevent.

inputs: An observed difference between Production behavior and its Git-tracked item definitions
processing: Diff the live Production item against its Git history
Determine whether the drift originated from a manual edit or an out-of-band change
Reconcile Production to a Git-tracked state and re-verify Gate 1
outputs: Production state that matches its tracked source of truth again
A documented root cause for the drift
Re-confirmed environment integrity before any further promotion
drill.example: A support engineer manually raises a Production capacity limit during an incident; once resolved, the change is captured back into the environment's tracked configuration instead of being left as an undocumented manual override.
failureModes: Manual Production fixes that are never reconciled back into Git
Drift discovered only when the next promotion overwrites the undocumented manual change

edges.label: yes — Deployment Pipelines and PR gate in place
yes — retries and idempotent writes proven under a forced failure
yes — secrets vaulted and permissions scoped to least privilege
no — environments not isolated or not Git-integrated
no — promotion is manual or has no PR gate
no — reliability pattern untested or duplicates on rerun
no — inline secrets or over-broad identity found
no — restore untested or no support owner confirmed
reconcile against Git-tracked baseline, re-open Gate 1

walkthrough.title: 1. Environments
walkthrough.explanation: Isolated, Git-integrated Dev/Test/Prod workspaces on the right workspace type are the foundation every later gate assumes exists.

walkthrough.title: 2. CI/CD
walkthrough.explanation: Deployment Pipelines with Variable Library binding and a pull-request gate turn promotion into a repeatable, reviewed process.

walkthrough.title: 3. Testing
walkthrough.explanation: A forced failure and rerun prove — rather than assume — that retries and idempotent MERGE writes actually protect the pipeline.

walkthrough.title: 4. Security
walkthrough.explanation: Vaulted secrets and least-privilege service identities bound both direct access and what Copilot and agents can surface.

walkthrough.title: 5. Operational readiness
walkthrough.explanation: A tested Item Recovery restore and a named support owner are the evidence that unlocks general availability.

walkthrough.title: Any gate can fail
walkthrough.explanation: A failed gate returns to that same phase for hardening; the workload never advances on an unresolved gap.

walkthrough.title: Drift returns to Gate 1
walkthrough.explanation: Configuration drift found in production is reconciled against the Git-tracked baseline, not patched in place.
